parsed.response: As the CEO of a major AI company, I would define accountability in AI governance as a binding and verifiable allocation of answerability across the AI lifecycle: named human and corporate actors must be able to explain, justify, and remedy the decisions and harms associated with AI systems they develop, procure, deploy, or operate, and must face consequences through regulators, courts, customers, and affected communities. Accountability is not liability alone and is not a property of a model; it is a governance relationship among legal persons. It has three layers: responsibility, meaning clear role-based duties; answerability, meaning documentation, transparency, audit, and incident reporting; and enforceability, meaning redress, sanctions, and legal liability. I would therefore reject vague calls for the system itself to be accountable and instead require a RACI-style allocation with a named accountable executive and legal entity for each high-risk system. The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) illustrates this role-based model: providers have duties under Article 16, deployers under Article 26, fundamental-rights impact assessments under Article 27 for specified deployers, post-market monitoring under Article 72, and serious-incident reporting under Article 73. GDPR adds data-protection accountability through Articles 5, 22, 24, 28, and 82, covering lawful processing, automated decision-making, processor contracts, and compensation. The Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (CETS 225) reinforces risk-based and rights-respecting answerability, while the OECD AI Principles, especially Principle 1.5 on accountability, and the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI supply the policy baseline that actors are accountable according to their roles and context. Operationally, I would align company governance with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, particularly its Govern function, and ISO/IEC 42001:2023 for an AI management system. Who or what should be accountable: providers and developers for safe design, data governance, conformity assessment, documentation, and monitoring; deployers and operators for context-specific risk assessment, human oversight, transparency to affected persons, and redress; executives and boards for resourcing, internal audit, and named ownership; and procurers and supply-chain actors for due diligence and contractual controls. AI models and systems are objects of documentation, evaluation, and control, not moral agents. For what: lawfulness and fundamental rights, safety and performance, transparency and explainability, data protection, non-discrimination, human oversight, security, incident response, and remedy. To whom: regulators and conformity bodies, courts, affected individuals and communities, workers and consumers, enterprise customers, shareholders, and the public. I would also use technical and procedural mechanisms such as documentation, model cards, bias audits, and reproducible evaluation, drawing on Kroll et al., Accountable Algorithms (2017), while recognizing Mittelstadt's warning that principles alone cannot guarantee ethical AI and Raji et al.'s argument for internal audit and closing the accountability gap. NYC Local Law 144 and State v. Loomis show how bias audits and due-process expectations around algorithmic evidence create concrete answerability, even where imperfect. My position as CEO is that accountability must be assigned before deployment, evidenced during operation, and enforceable after harm.

parsed.response: As CEO, I would frame enforceability as the ability of a legal regime to turn an AI governance norm into a binding, observable, contestable, and remediable obligation. It has six elements: (1) legal basis and obligation — a statute, treaty, or contract creating a duty rather than a recommendation; (2) precision and operationalization — defined duty-bearers, triggers, thresholds, timelines, and acceptable evidence; (3) verification — audits, documentation, conformity assessment, incident reporting, and regulator access; (4) enforcement institutions — a regulator, court, procurement authority, or certification body with powers to inspect, order, fine, suspend, or grant relief; (5) remedies and due process — penalties, injunctions, damages, appeals, and rights to contest; and (6) de facto capacity — funding, technical expertise, and cross-border cooperation. A rule is merely aspirational when it uses hortatory language, lacks measurable duties or evidence, leaves compliance to self-assessment, and provides no standing, sanction, or remedy. Enforceability is a spectrum, not binary: hard law can be unenforceable if vague or under-resourced, while soft law can become enforceable through contracts, procurement conditions, certification, or incorporation by reference. The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) is enforceable in design because it creates prohibitions, high-risk provider obligations, conformity assessment and CE marking, market-surveillance authorities, and fines up to EUR 35 million or 7% of global turnover; its actual enforceability will depend on harmonized standards and national regulator capacity. GDPR Art. 22 and Art. 83 are enforceable through data-protection authorities and courts, and CJEU C-634/21 (SCHUFA) shows that automated credit scoring can be an Art. 22 decision, making transparency and human review justiciable. In the US, FTC Act Section 5 supports unfair or deceptive-practices enforcement, as in the FTC's Rite Aid facial-recognition order; Title VII supports disparate-impact liability; and NYC Local Law 144 and Colorado SB 24-205 create audit and impact-assessment duties. By contrast, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework is voluntary and aspirational unless a contract or procurement rule incorporates it. Loomis v. Wisconsin (Wis. 2016) illustrates procedural due-process limits on algorithmic risk scores but did not create a general AI rule. ECHR cases such as Glukhin v. Russia and the Dutch SyRI judgment show rights-based enforceability through courts requiring legal basis, necessity, and transparency. The Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (CETS 225) is a treaty with obligations, but its practical force depends on domestic implementation and monitoring. OECD AI Principles and UNESCO's Recommendation are soft law. Theoretically, Abbott et al.'s legalization framework is useful: obligation, precision, and delegation determine whether a norm is hard or soft, and a rule with high obligation but low precision and low delegation is often aspirational in practice. Responsive regulation (Ayres and Braithwaite) and risk-based new-governance approaches explain how enforceable regimes combine ex ante controls, audit, and escalating sanctions. As CEO, I would support enforceable, interoperable, risk-based rules with clear safe harbors, third-party audits, incident reporting, and regulator capacity, because predictable enforcement is better for innovation than vague principles that expose companies to unpredictable liability.

Legal certainty, as it applies to AI systems used in public decision-making, is the rule-of-law requirement that the legal basis for those systems, and the way they classify, score, prioritize, or recommend outcomes for individuals, be clear, accessible, stable, and foreseeable enough that people can anticipate how public power may affect them, rely on that understanding, and effectively challenge unlawful or arbitrary results. It does not require publication of every model parameter. It requires that automation not become a substitute for knowable law.

It requires several things. First, an accessible legal basis that states the system's purpose, the decisions it may inform, and the limits of its use. Under the European Court of Human Rights' quality-of-law doctrine in Sunday Times v. United Kingdom (1979), a norm counts as law only if it is formulated with sufficient precision for people to foresee, to a degree reasonable in the circumstances, the consequences of their conduct. The Venice Commission's Rule of Law Checklist (CDL-AD(2016)007) treats accessibility, foreseeability, stability, consistency, and protection of legitimate expectations as benchmarks of legal certainty. Second, the operative rules must themselves be clear and precise. The Court of Justice of the European Union, in Case 169/80 Gondrand Freres (1981), held that legal certainty requires rules of law to be clear and precise and their application foreseeable by those subject to them. Handing material criteria to an opaque or continually retuned model, without stable and published rules, fails that test. Third, people need proportionate information about the data categories used, the system's role in the decision, and the logic applied, plus reasons and a real route to review. The GDPR (Articles 5, 13-15, and 22) requires transparency and, for solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, safeguards that include meaningful information about the logic involved. The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) imposes record-keeping, transparency, and human-oversight duties on high-risk systems, including specified public-sector uses. French administrative law (Code des relations entre le public et l'administration, Article L. 311-3-1) gives individuals a right to the rules and principal characteristics of algorithmic processing that underlies an individual administrative decision. Article 41 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights requires good administration, including reasons. The Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (CETS No. 225) ties public use of AI to the rule of law, transparency, accountability, and effective remedies. Fourth, material changes to models, thresholds, or criteria should not be applied retroactively to people who reasonably relied on the prior published framework. Danielle Keats Citron's Technological Due Process (2008) makes the related point that rules embedded in government code undermine notice and the opportunity to be heard when neither officials nor affected people can inspect them.

Legal certainty is absent when a public body cannot explain, and a person cannot reasonably predict or reconstruct, why a benefit was denied, a risk flag raised, or a sanction proposed; when similarly situated people are treated inconsistently without a lawful justification; or when secrecy, proprietary or otherwise, blocks a challenge to accuracy, relevance, or bias. The District Court of The Hague's 2020 SyRI judgment (NJCM and others v. the State of the Netherlands) invalidated a welfare-fraud risk-profiling system in part because its operation was insufficiently transparent and foreseeable to satisfy Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. State v. Loomis, 881 N.W.2d 749 (Wis. 2016), shows the same tension in sentencing: a proprietary risk tool may inform a decision only within due-process limits, and inability to examine how it weighs factors strains the person's capacity to contest the result. In that condition, automation does not merely implement the law; it hides the law.

parsed.response:
Accountability in AI governance is a relational and institutional duty, not a property of a model. Following Mark Bovens, it is a relationship in which an actor must explain and justify conduct to a forum that can question, judge, and impose consequences. Applied to AI, the relationship has to be specified across the lifecycle: who the actor is, for which decisions and harms, before which forum, and with what remedies. Technical explainability is only one means; documentation, traceability, oversight, and redress are equally necessary.

Who should be accountable. Duties should attach to identifiable legal persons who exercise control, allocated by role rather than to “the algorithm.” Providers (those who develop a system or place it on the market) bear primary duties for design, training-data governance, testing, technical documentation, and instructions for use. Deployers (those who use a system under their authority) bear primary duties for whether the system is appropriate to the context, for human oversight, for how outputs are acted on, and for monitoring in operation. Importers, distributors, and operators of general-purpose or high-risk systems bear duties proportionate to their control and knowledge. Individuals inside organizations remain answerable through corporate governance, professional standards, and, in serious cases, personal liability, but a model cannot itself be a duty-bearer. States and regulators are accountable for the quality, independence, and effectiveness of oversight, not for every private deployment outcome.

For what. Accountability should cover: (1) design and development choices, including data governance, risk assessment, and evaluation; (2) deployment decisions, including fitness for context, human oversight, and instructions to users; (3) ongoing operation, logging, incident reporting, and correction or withdrawal when performance or impacts degrade; (4) compliance with applicable law, including data protection, non-discrimination, consumer and product-safety rules, and sectoral duties; and (5) harms to fundamental rights, safety, and legitimate interests, including where causation is probabilistic or mediated by a human decision-maker. Duties should scale with risk and with the degree of control, not with whether the system is labeled “AI.”

To whom. Affected persons—data subjects, consumers, workers, patients, and others whose rights or interests are engaged—should have rights to information, to an explanation adequate to the decision context, to human review of significant decisions, and to an effective remedy. Independent regulators and courts are the principal public forums, with powers to investigate, order correction, and impose sanctions. Where public bodies deploy AI, democratic institutions, auditors, and ombudsmen are additional forums. Because many harms are collective, individual standing should be supplemented by public-interest and collective mechanisms.

This allocation is already partly codified. The EU AI Act distinguishes providers and deployers and imposes risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, transparency, human oversight, and post-market monitoring, with market-surveillance authorities as a forum and penalties as consequences. The GDPR’s accountability principle in Article 5(2), the controller/processor structure, transparency and access rights in Articles 13–15, constraints on solely automated decisions in Article 22, and data-protection impact assessments in Article 35 allocate duties for personal-data processing and give data subjects and supervisory authorities standing. The OECD AI Principles and the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI treat accountability as a lifecycle governance principle requiring traceability and human oversight. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework operationalizes related functions (govern, map, measure, manage) without itself creating liability. The Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence requires parties to maintain accountability and redress for AI harms to human rights, democracy, and the rule of law. Case law such as State v. Loomis shows courts already functioning as forums when algorithmic tools affect liberty, while also showing the limits of disclosure as a substitute for answerability.

Scholarly work supplies the conceptual constraints. Bovens distinguishes accountability from mere transparency. Helen Nissenbaum identified how computerized systems fragment responsibility so that no one can be called to account. Wachter, Mittelstadt, and Floridi caution that a freestanding “right to explanation” is easily overstated and does not by itself produce remedy. Selbst and Barocas show that intuitive demands for explanation can miss the institutional question of who must justify what to whom. A sound framework therefore combines ex ante duties (risk and impact assessment, documentation, human oversight), ex post duties (logging, incident reporting, audit, liability, and remedy), and clear forums, allocated by control and role.

Enforceability, applied to AI regulation, is the property that turns a norm into a duty whose breach can be detected, adjudicated, and remedied by an institution with legal authority. It is not the same as moral force, political consensus, or reputational pressure. A rule is enforceable when four conditions hold together: it is adopted in a form the legal system recognizes as binding; it imposes determinate obligations on identifiable actors; a competent authority has jurisdiction plus powers to investigate and decide; and non-compliance can end in a compulsory outcome—an order, penalty, injunction, market exclusion, or damages—that can actually be executed. An aspirational rule states goals or recommended practices without creating justiciable obligations or sanctions. Mandatory-sounding language does not by itself make a text enforceable.

Legal theory supplies the distinction. H.L.A. Hart treated law as a union of primary rules of obligation and secondary rules of recognition, change, and adjudication. Many AI ethics codes have primary-looking principles but no secondary rules that tell officials what counts as law or how disputes are decided. Lon Fuller’s account of legality adds operational tests: generality, promulgation, clarity, consistency, possibility of compliance, stability, and congruence between official action and the declared rule. Open slogans such as “trustworthy” or “human-centric” AI fail clarity and congruence unless they are operationalized. Kenneth Abbott and Duncan Snidal’s hard-law/soft-law framework is especially useful for AI governance: instruments vary by obligation (binding versus hortatory), precision (determinate versus vague), and delegation (to a court, regulator, or monitoring body). Soft law can shape expectations and later legislation, but it is not enforceable on its own. Anu Bradford’s Brussels Effect explains a further practical dimension: market-access conditions can make formally territorial rules de facto binding on foreign firms that want to sell into the regulating market.

Binding instruments show what enforceability looks like in AI-relevant law. The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) is the clearest contemporary example of hard AI law: it prohibits specified practices, imposes duties on providers and deployers of high-risk systems and on general-purpose AI models, uses conformity assessment and market surveillance, and authorizes substantial administrative fines (including, for prohibited practices, up to €35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover). The GDPR is already an enforceable constraint on many AI systems that process personal data: independent supervisory authorities, investigative powers, administrative fines up to €20 million or 4% of global turnover, private judicial remedies, and Article 22 limits on solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects. In the United States, enforceability is more fragmented. NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework is voluntary guidance; it becomes enforceable only if a statute, procurement rule, or contract incorporates it. State measures such as Colorado’s SB 24-205 and New York City Local Law 144 create more concrete duties, documentation or audit requirements, and public enforcement, though scope and remedies differ. Loomis v. Wisconsin (2016) shows courts engaging algorithmic risk scores under due process, and also the limit of judicial enforceability where trade secrecy and the absence of a statutory transparency duty constrain what a court will order.

By contrast, the OECD AI Principles and the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI are soft-law benchmarks. They coordinate policy and supply a vocabulary for later law, but they do not themselves impose sanctions or private rights of action. The Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law is different in form: as a treaty it can create international legal obligations for parties, yet many duties are framed at a high level of generality, so practical enforceability depends on domestic implementation, monitoring, and whatever remedies national law supplies.

The operational contrast is therefore this. An enforceable AI rule names the obligor (provider, deployer, importer, public authority), states a standard that can be evidenced (logs, risk management, conformity assessment, bias audit, human oversight), designates a forum (regulator, court, or both), and attaches a remedy (fine, injunction, withdrawal, liability). An aspirational rule addresses “stakeholders,” uses unoperationalized values, relies on voluntary codes or certification, and treats compliance as a matter of reputation. A useful test: if an actor can ignore the text without facing a compulsory process that can end in a binding order or penalty, the text remains aspirational even if it uses the word “shall.” Conversely, a principle becomes enforceable when legislation, contract, or judicial doctrine supplies an obligor, a standard of conduct, a forum, and a remedy—and when the state has the capacity to monitor systems that are opaque, cross-border, and rapidly updated. Formal bindingness without monitoring capacity yields only weak enforceability; precision and institutional capacity are what separate a governable rule from a statement of intent.

parsed.response: As the CEO of a major AI company in this working group, I define legal certainty for AI used in public decision-making as the practical ability of an affected person, the responsible official, and a reviewing court to know in advance which rules govern an AI-assisted decision, to foresee how those rules will be applied to like cases, and to obtain a reviewable account of why a particular outcome was reached. It is a rule-of-law requirement, not a demand that every model weight be published. It requires four things. First, a clear and accessible legal mandate: the authority to deploy the system, the purposes for which it may be used, and the interests it may affect must be set in law, not left to a procurement memo. Second, foreseeable and consistent application, so that similarly situated people can expect similar treatment and so that model, threshold, or data changes are versioned and documented rather than silent. Third, reason-giving sufficient for legality review—under the EU AI Act’s high-risk duties on transparency, logging, and human oversight; under GDPR Article 22’s limits on solely automated decisions that produce legal or similarly significant effects; and under constitutional due-process duties of the kind examined in State v. Loomis. Fourth, an effective remedy: notice, access to the material factors, and a human decision-maker who can depart from the system’s output and be held accountable for the decision. When legal certainty is absent, a benefits agency, court, or border authority relies on a proprietary score whose factors, thresholds, and error rates are undisclosed; officials can say only that “the system decided”; like cases diverge without a recorded reason; and the person affected cannot tell whether the result was lawful, biased, or the product of an unannounced software update. That is the breakdown Danielle Keats Citron called a failure of technological due process, and it is the concern that the Venice Commission’s Rule of Law Checklist treats as the core of legal certainty: law must be clear, stable, and predictable, and applied consistently. From an industry seat I will be plain: vendors must not sell opacity as a feature into the exercise of public power. Certainty is a design and contracting requirement—logged inputs, versioned models, contestable reasons, and terms that do not forbid the state from explaining its own decisions.

parsed.response: Accountability in AI governance is the enforceable duty to answer for how an AI system is designed, deployed, monitored, and remediated across its lifecycle. It is allocated by control and risk, not by brand alone. Providers should be accountable for model design choices, training-data governance, technical documentation, and known safety and rights controls. Deployers should be accountable for the context of use, human oversight, and impacts on affected people. Public authorities should be accountable for proportionate, predictable rules and enforcement. People and organizations subject to high-risk or rights-impacting systems should be able to seek explanation, contestation, and redress. Where control is split, responsibility should be shared and documented rather than left in an accountability gap. This position tracks the EU AI Act's provider and deployer duties, the GDPR accountability principle and limits on solely automated decisions, the OECD AI Principles' accountability pillar, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework's Govern function, and the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law.

From the standpoint of a company that will have to build, document, and defend systems under whatever framework this group produces, enforceability is not a rhetorical preference for toughness. It is the set of institutional features that turn a norm into a duty a regulated party can understand, a supervisor can test, and a court or authority can apply with predictable consequences. An enforceable AI rule changes conduct because noncompliance carries a real prospect of detection, correction, and sanction. An aspirational rule expresses a value—fairness, human-centricity, trustworthiness—without specifying who must do what, how compliance is shown, or what happens if it is not.

Five features mark the difference. First, an identifiable duty-bearer: provider, deployer, importer, or public authority, not an undefined ecosystem. Second, an obligation specific enough to guide conduct and evidence—prohibited practices, risk-management and documentation duties, conformity assessment, logging, incident reporting, or transparency to affected persons—rather than an outcome no current method can measure, such as perfect fairness or zero error. Third, a competent authority with investigative and corrective powers, and a stated remedy: administrative fines, withdrawal or recall, injunctive relief, or civil liability. Fourth, procedure: standards of proof, rights of defense, and appeal, so enforcement itself is lawful. Fifth, possibility of compliance. A mandate that cannot be operationalized is aspiration wearing statutory clothing; it produces discretionary enforcement, not the rule of law.

Binding instruments already show the pattern. The EU AI Act is a regulation with direct effect, a risk-based allocation of duties, market-surveillance authorities, and substantial administrative fines; whether one agrees with every obligation, the enforcement architecture is recognizable. The GDPR supplies the nearer precedent for cross-border digital regulation: independent supervisory authorities, turnover-based fines, and data-subject remedies, which is why firms treat it as law rather than guidance. In the United States, much AI-relevant enforcement still attaches to older, genuinely enforceable statutes—the FTC Act’s prohibition on unfair or deceptive practices has been used against misleading AI claims—rather than to a comprehensive AI code. State v. Loomis is a different but instructive constraint: due process limits how opaque algorithmic tools may be used when liberty is at stake. It enforces a constitutional boundary on government use; it does not itself create a private-sector compliance regime.

Soft law sits on the other side of the line, and it is not useless. The OECD AI Principles and the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence shape expectations and often migrate into later statutes, but they create no justiciable duty and no penalty. NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework is technically serious and widely used; adherence may evidence diligence, yet non-adherence is not, by itself, a violation. Executive directives can bind agencies inside government while leaving private duties incomplete. Voluntary codes and principles-based charters belong in the aspirational category unless a legislature or regulator later incorporates them into a standard that can be audited and sanctioned.

Theory draws the same line. H.L.A. Hart’s account of law distinguishes primary rules of obligation from secondary rules of recognition, change, and adjudication: a principle becomes enforceable only when institutions can identify it as law, apply it to cases, and back it with official pressure. Lon Fuller’s criteria for the inner morality of law—clarity, consistency, prospectivity, possibility of compliance, and congruence between the rule as announced and the rule as applied—are practical tests for this working group. A standard that fails those tests will be enforced unevenly or not at all, which is worse for both safety and innovation than an explicitly voluntary principle.

For governance design, the implication is selective bindingness. Use enforceable rules where harm is serious and duties can be specified and audited: bans on defined unacceptable practices, documented risk management for high-risk uses, human oversight where a statute assigns it, incident reporting, and truthful claims about capabilities. Keep principles, benchmarks, and maturity models explicitly non-binding where measurement is unstable, so that enforcement does not collapse into after-the-fact taste. Enforceability, in short, is specificity plus institutions plus consequences. Aspiration is a direction of travel. Both have a place; confusing them produces neither safety nor legal certainty.
